name: Forest green
lede: Forest green is a strong, mid-dark green named for woodland; as a screen color it is the web's ForestGreen, and the name itself was already in English use by 1810.

sections.title: Two things with one name
sections.body:
Paterson separates the traditional color from the web one. Forest-green, in his dictionary, is an olive green slightly darker than Lincoln green, sometimes yellowish and sometimes a dark muted green [1]. ForestGreen, written as one word, is one of the X11 colors with the hex code #228B22 [1]. The swatch here is the X11 one [1].

The measured swatch reads as a strong yellowish green in ISCC-NBS terms, block 125, and also appears in Ridgway's 1912 plates and in Maerz and Paul [2]. Our data places the first use of the name as a color in English at about 1810 [3]. Nearby greens are [[hunter-green]], [[dark-green]], [[pine-green]], [[fern-green]] and [[kelly-green]].

sections.title: In the books
sections.body: The books mention it only in passing, as a plain adjective. Finlay, for example, describes the forest-green cast-metal frame of an old Hattersley loom in a Scottish mill [4]. The word works as common description, not as a pigment with a documented history.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive has this exact green covering as much as 1 percent of its canvas, as photographed [5]. That describes our archive, not painting as a whole, and dark painted greens usually shift toward olive and brown with varnish. In printed English the phrase forest green rose fastest from the 1990s and peaks in the 2010s in Google Books, all senses included [5].

origin.first_recorded: about 1810 as an English color name
